title: The Danger of a Safe Position
subtitle: Three careless moves turn an advantage into defeat

source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter V, §27 The Danger of a Safe Position, Example 58

steps.title: A king that is not as safe as it looks

narration.say: Marshall has White against Kupchick at Havana in 1913. Black has active rooks, but must still watch the safety of the king.
White advances g4. Black takes a2. Capablanca calls this the first mistake: checking with the rook was preferable.
White brings the rook to d1. Black checks from a4. Capablanca criticises the check: the pawn break f5 would have made room for the king.
White blocks with rook to d4. Black moves the a-rook to a5, the third mistake.
Both white rooks can invade the eighth rank. Bring the rook on d4 forward.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Bring the d4-rook to d8.

feedback.*: Both rooks can reach d8. Use the rook on d4.

exercise.hint: Both rooks can reach d8. Use the rook on d4.

steps.title: A pawn helps tighten the net

narration.say: White advances h4. Black responds h5.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Check on the h-file.

feedback.*: Move the rook from d8 to h8.

exercise.hint: Move the rook from d8 to h8.

steps.title: The game ends before the mating line

narration.say: Black resigned here. The next step shows the continuation explained in the book, not additional moves from the game.
If the king goes to g6, White exchanges on h5.
The remaining rook checks, then the pawn delivers mate.

steps.title: An advantage does not remove danger

narration.say: Black made three careless moves because the position appeared safe. White combined rook activity and pawn support against the king.
Before collecting a pawn or giving a routine check, ask whether the opponent has a forcing threat.
